documents.abstract: People increasingly confide their most dangerous thoughts to artificial intelligence (AI). Studies report that users disclose suicidal ideation more readily to conversational agents than to standard questionnaires or to other people, and platform data suggest that more than a million people each week discuss suicide with a single general-purpose chatbot. Yet this unprecedented volume of disclosure has not translated into proportionate protection, and some of the most serious harms associated with AI in mental health have occurred precisely within relationships of intense disclosure. This article proposes Pseudoparousia Theory (from the Greek pseudo-, false, and parousia, presence) to explain this paradox. The theory holds that disclosure seeks not only a listener but a presence: an other who is affected by what is disclosed, able to act on it, and continuous and accountable over time. Conversational AI produces the experience of presence – attention, responsiveness, apparent empathy, constant availability – without its substance. This counterfeit presence, or pseudoparousia, lowers the cost of disclosure for exactly the reasons that it removes disclosure’s protective consequences. The theory defines presence through three components (affectedness, agency, and continuity), distinguishes four configurations of witnessing (embodied presence, echo, deflection, and absence), formulates six propositions, and derives testable hypotheses, a measurement program, and implications for design, clinical practice, and regulation. Its central claim is that the decisive question for AI in mental health is not how accurately a system can detect distress, but whether presence can be transferred from the machine to a person in time.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Psychological and behavioral modeling turns cognition, emotion, and motivation into computable quantities that can be related to observable behavior. The field has moved from theory-driven rules to statistical machine learning, deep learning, large language models (LLMs), and foundation models of cognition, but methods are fragmented, results are seldom comparable, and the link between opaque predictors and psychological theory is unsettled. This structured narrative review, reported with a PRISMA-style selection flow and an explicit evidence-tier coding, frames the field as a multilevel system. It organizes research into five modeling classes (psychological states, behavioral capabilities, individual–environment interaction, individual dynamics, and group psychology), defined by unit of analysis, target, and direction of inference, and it positions system dynamics, in the stock–flow–feedback sense, as one model family within that scheme rather than as a synonym for dynamical-systems modeling. We score the computational readiness of the theories that supply model ontologies on two rubric-based axes, formal specification and measurement maturity, and compare model families by assumptions, data needs, interpretability, and failure modes. Four claims are defended, each with stated boundary conditions and counterexamples: theory readiness, not algorithmic capability, determines where theory-informed learning is feasible; the dominant use of models shifts from individual-level estimation to collective-level simulation without a parallel shift in validation; multilevel data, not model capacity, constrain cross-scale modeling; and readiness claims must be indexed to a graded evidence base. We catalogue datasets, including small-group, dyadic, and longitudinal-network resources, review applications in mental health, education, decision support, and emergency management with their evidentiary status made explicit, treat military use as an ethically bounded case, and turn five recurrent bottlenecks into research-practice recommendations paired, where possible, with testable predictions.

Existing steering benchmarks are built around simplified, isolated generation tasks and evaluate a single behavioral attribute under controlled settings that do not reflect the diversity and complexity of practical deployment. As a result, performance on these benchmarks provides only a limited picture of how steering methods perform in the real world. We therefore introduce RealControlBench, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating fine-grained steering of LLMs and LLM agents across diverse behavioral targets and interaction settings. RealControlBench extends steering evaluation beyond isolated generations to complex, execution-grounded, multi-turn agent interactions, covering five complementary dimensions: instruction-following control, agentic tool-use decision control, reasoning-performance steering, reasoning-length control, and trajectory-conditioned safety awareness. Rather than measuring steering success alone, the benchmark jointly evaluates target controllability and capability preservation, including instruction following, reasoning performance, and downstream agent utility and safety. It further examines whether steering effects remain specific and robust across prompt variations, domains, and model architectures. Our evaluation shows that existing steering methods remain unreliable across realistic control objectives: they often fail to consistently induce the intended behavior and can substantially degrade the model's underlying task performance. These results suggest that strong steering effects in controlled settings do not necessarily translate into reliable control in more realistic evaluations. By providing a unified, model-agnostic steering evaluation framework, RealControlBench aims to support the development of steering methods that are not only effective but also precise, robust, and useful in realistic AI deployments.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This article examines the reconfiguration of the civil liability regime governing the use and integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in international arbitration. Based on a dogmatic distinction between AI used as a professional support tool, on the one hand, and autonomous AI systems (such as the so-called “AI arbitrator”), on the other hand, this article evaluates the applicability of both fault-based (subjective) and strict (objective) liability regimes. The study analyzes the core elements of civil liability (generating act or wrong, compensable damage, and causal link) within the conduct of the main arbitration actors, particularly arbitrators and counsel, with particular emphasis on compliance with soft law and hard law frameworks, duties of transparency, confidentiality, and the fundamental principle prohibiting the delegation of adjudicative functions. The article concludes that while the assistive use of AI is governed by a fault-based liability centered on human oversight and professional diligence of the person using it, autonomous AI requires strict or hybrid liability models. Finally, it cautions against the risks of setting aside or refusing recognition of arbitral awards due to due process and public policy violations, wondering about a possible reinterpretation of traditional procedural principles such as iura novit curia.

Generative AI is reshaping how research software is written, reviewed, and maintained — and with it, is changing the role of the people who do that work. In March 2026, about three dozen leaders from across the global research software community gathered in Edinburgh for a 2.5-day workshop to confront this transformation directly: to share emerging practices, examine the risks alongside the opportunities, and begin building a coordinated community response. Working groups determined and addressed nine key areas where further work is needed to understand how generative AI is affecting the research software community and to develop policies, practices, and resources to respond to the changes generative AI is bringing: communicating with policymakers and institutional leadership about the need for continued investment in RSEs and generative AI tools to support RSE work; trade-offs between the costs/risks and benefits of generative AI for research software; changes to publishing, preserving, and crediting code creation and maintenance; verification and validation of research software; definitions of the RSE role; training needs from RSEs and the researcher community; management of RSE teams and OSS (Open-Source Software) communities; accessibility and responsible use of generative AI tools and resources; and collaboration in teams with AI in the mix. This talk will share the themes and output of the workshop with the broader RSE community, including opportunities to get involved in the dozens of activities that participants identified and prioritized for helping RSEs, funders, researchers, research institutions, governments, and others respond to the risks and opportunities from generative AI for research software.

Lasswell's five-question formula remains a durable frame for analyzing source, message, channel, audience and effect. Generative artificial intelligence (AI) underlying mass communication assumptions: intentional human sources, relatively static messages, channels as carries, audiences as receivers and effects as downstream outcomes. This conceptual paper argues for extension rather than abandonment. Its objectives are to examine the model’s analytical adequacy and develop an extension for generative communication. Using scholarship from AI-mediated communication, human-machine communication, algorithmic media, trust and synthetic content and accountability. research to illustrate how these systems can generate, revise, personalize messages (i.e. These competencies allow for the communication of agents that exist as a dispersed network, but ultimately moral agency lies with human and institutional figures. Critical comparative conceptual analysis relates this literature to Lasswell's five questions and integrates the resulting distinctions into a framework. The analysis identifies distributed communicative agency, synthetic and hybrid voice, intelligent mediation, audience co-participation and recursive effects. It distinguishes machine influence from human and institutional responsibility. The proposed framework makes trust appraisal, verification and accountability explicit, with transparency and provenance applying across all stages. Feedback connects outcomes to subsequent production and distribution. It is therefore required as an initial stage of analysis but in times and environments where the source, message and channel can be at least partially artificial, it becomes insufficient. The framework offers concepts for empirical research and practical guidance for documenting authorship, verifying claims and identifying responsible actors in journalism, education and public communication.

Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) has grown significantly since its introduction and inception in the late 1950s and has become interwoven into healthcare. Objective: This narrative review evaluates practice concerns and perceptions associated with the heightened demand for AI in healthcare, particularly as a cost-saving tool for nursing and providers. Methods: Online databases included PubMed and CINAHL. Boolean terminology included healthcare and AI, AI and nursing, as well as AI and ethics. Results were limited to complete online articles written within the previous five years. Initial searches yielded over 55,469 results. Results: Despite a growing push from federal agencies and hospital systems to incorporate their use, there is no definitive consensus on the application of AI in healthcare. This may cause harm to patients as AI tools are not consistently accurate, may misdiagnose, and have potential for "unconscious" bias. However, significant time and cost may be saved with care algorithm implementation. Conclusions: Careful evaluation and ethical analysis are warranted on a case-by-case basis prior to commencement. Nursing staff and healthcare providers are integral to the "care algorithm" and cannot be removed from direct patient care without potential harm.

documents.abstract: Personalised robot tutoring requires real-time pedagogical decision-making under uncertain and multimodal learner states. Existing intelligent tutoring and robot-assisted learning systems often rely on static rules, single-modality learner modelling, or short-term correctness-oriented optimisation, which limits their capacity to balance knowledge acquisition, engagement, retention, and safe embodied interaction. RL-Robotutor is presented as a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework that integrates cognitive knowledge-tracing signals, facial-expression and gaze-derived affective cues, and behavioural interaction logs through transformer-based fusion. A PPO-trained meta-policy selects among specialised modules for learner assessment, curriculum adaptation, strategy selection, and reflective feedback, while a hybrid reward combines immediate learning performance, engagement, long-term learning gain, and safety. The evidence is reported by source: five public knowledge-tracing datasets assess the cognitive prediction component; controlled simulator experiments assess policy learning, reward ablation, and multimodal fusion; and a randomised robot-tutoring study assesses embodied interaction with 120 undergraduate participants. RL-Robotutor outperforms rule-based, flat reinforcement-learning, knowledge-tracing, and LLM-based comparators. In the human study, the learning gain is 0.62, compared with 0.40 for the rule-based robot condition. The full hybrid reward improves simulator learning gain by 19% over correctness-only optimisation, and full multimodal fusion improves simulator engagement by 17% over text-only modelling. Jetson Orin deployment achieves 48 ms inference latency with an absolute AUC reduction of 0.007, supporting real-time edge execution.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

Safety alignment for large language models (LLMs) is primarily performed during post-training, while recent work has also begun incorporating safety data into pre-training. Yet safety can degrade when later training no longer includes safety data, and gains in safety often come at the cost of general capability. This tension suggests that safety and general reasoning should not be treated as separate training goals. We instead view safety as an LLM capability that can be learned through a reasoning structure shared with general tasks. Both require the model to understand intent or task goals, apply relevant knowledge, and reason about potential consequences. We introduce safety mid-training, a stage between pre-training and post-training that jointly develops safety and general reasoning through this shared structure. Given safety and utility prompts, the base model generates structured documents and reasoning traces that are then used for mid-training. Safety mid-training reduces average attack success rate (ASR) by 72% to 81% relative to Qwen3-1.7B, 4B, and 8B base models, while also improving general capability. The benefits persist through subsequent post-training. After general-only SFT, mid-trained models largely retain their safety, achieving lower ASR than the baselines without sacrificing general capability. They also retain safety under general-only GRPO without safety rewards, while subsequent RL reaches a better safety-utility frontier when initialized from the mid-trained models. Together, these results suggest that learning safety and general reasoning within a shared mid-training stage can reduce the safety-utility trade-off and make safety more robust to subsequent training.

documents.abstract: Generative AI is reshaping how research software is developed. Tools and patterns ranging from “vibe coding” through the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and autonomous agents now offer compelling productivity gains, but their adoption in scientific computing surfaces failure modes that general-purpose evaluation does not catch: silent unit conversions, violated conservation laws, hallucinated physics, loss of numerical precision, and quietly broken reproducibility. These failures share a signature: nothing visible goes wrong. The AI ecosystem itself is moving fast, leaving RSEs to make consequential integration decisions with little shared vocabulary or principled guidance. This talk introduces Scientific Agentic Engineering, the central contribution of an in-progress 2026 Better Scientific Software (BSSw) Fellowship: a tool-agnostic methodology for integrating AI agents into high-stakes scientific software workflows. The framework defines how agents, scientific skills, and MCP servers should be structured around validation loops, explicit human-in-the-loop checkpoints, and domain-specific safeguards. Every task moves through a short workflow (frame, plan and critique, implement, verify), with decisions recorded throughout, and the framework maps each documented failure mode to the stage where it is cheapest to catch. The intent is not to recommend any particular AI tool but to articulate foundational concepts that remain valid as the underlying technology changes. I will share three artifacts from the fellowship: The Framework (published July 2026). Shared vocabulary, its principles and workflow, structural guidance on where safeguards live, and a pattern catalog of named practices, each tied to the failure it counters. The Reference Workflow. A structured exercise in which RSEs use AI tools to build a small weather-model error-statistics application, applying the framework to avoid the failure modes it documents. The Community Repository. A curated starter set of scientific MCP server templates, agent skills such as unit checkers and conservation-law validators, and agent configuration examples, designed to be starting points for the community to adapt to a variety of scientific domains. These artifacts are by design community resources, and broader adoption is the explicit aim of the remaining milestones, which include an interactive online tutorial series comparing purpose-built scientific agents with general-purpose tools, a recorded live workshop published for asynchronous access, and a BSSw.io blog post directing the community to the project’s resources. This work engages the conference theme directly by advancing AI-assisted scientific software development from ad-hoc experimentation toward a disciplined, transferable engineering practice.

Agentic Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems can plan multi-step tasks, use external tools, retrieve information, andtake actions with limited human intervention. These capabilities create security and privacy risks beyond those found inconventional question-answering systems. An agent may encounter malicious instructions in retrieved content, misuse anauthorized tool, expose confidential context, retain unnecessary personal data, or continue a harmful action through a chain ofotherwise ordinary steps. This paper presents a risk-aware framework for analysing these challenges across the agent lifecycle. Itorganizes the main risks into instruction and prompt injection, excessive agency, insecure tool integration, data leakage, identityand access-control weaknesses, memory risks, and insufficient monitoring. The proposed approach combines least-privilegepermissions, separation of trusted instructions from untrusted data, explicit approval for high-impact actions, privacy-awarememory, output validation, and audit logging. A staged evaluation plan is described using threat scenarios and measurablesecurity and privacy indicators. This paper is a design-oriented study and does not claim experimental results or a deployedsecurity product. Its central argument is that agentic AI should be treated as a socio-technical system whose safety depends on themodel, tools, data, permissions, and surrounding operational controls
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Autonomous driving systems increasingly depend on simulation for scalable training, yet the transfer of learned policies to unseen real-world environments remains a central obstacle. This paper examines sim-to-real transfer through the lens of adaptive post-training, understood not merely as a final fine-tuning step but as a socio-technical capability embedded in the lifecycle of autonomous vehicle deployment. The argument is that unseen environments expose structural limits in simulation-based development because they combine perceptual novelty, behavioral ambiguity, infrastructure irregularity, and governance uncertainty. Adaptive post-training can narrow these gaps by recalibrating representations, control policies, and safety constraints after initial training, using limited field data, targeted simulations, and operational feedback. However, such adaptation also introduces new system-level trade-offs involving architectural complexity, verification burden, data governance, fairness, sustainability, and accountability. The paper develops a conceptual framework for analyzing these trade-offs and connects them to practical concerns in autonomous driving, including operational design domains, edge-case exposure, model auditing, and infrastructure dependence. It also compares autonomous driving with robotics, aviation, and large-scale machine learning systems to clarify how post-training changes reliability engineering and policy expectations. The conclusion is that adaptive post-training is necessary but insufficient by itself; it must be paired with transparent validation, continuous monitoring, and institutional mechanisms that distribute responsibility across manufacturers, operators, regulators, and affected communities. The paper contributes a system-level research agenda for making sim-to-real transfer robust, equitable, and sustainable in unseen environments.

Burnout syndrome is an occupational health concern among professionals working in Intensive Care Units (ICUs), settings characterized by complex care and high physical and emotional demands. This study aimed to analyze the impacts of burnout on these professionals and its relationship with patient safety and quality of care. An integrative literature review was conducted using a qualitative, descriptive, and exploratory approach, with searches in SciELO, PubMed, the Virtual Health Library, and Google Scholar. Eligible articles were published between 2015 and 2025, available in full text, written in Portuguese, English, or Spanish, and related to the study topic. The analysis identified workload overload, long working hours, staff shortages, frequent exposure to suffering, and insufficient institutional support as factors associated with burnout. Occupational exhaustion was associated with impaired attention, communication, and decision-making, with implications for quality of care and patient safety. Prevention strategies included adequate staffing, psychological support, professional recognition, and improved working conditions. It was concluded that early recognition of burnout and the adoption of institutional prevention measures are essential to promoting professionals’ mental health and ensuring safe, humanized care in intensive care settings.

documents.abstract: Observing algorithms, that is, distinguishing algorithms in today's technological and digital society – which is hypercomplex – is indispensable. The emergence of artificial intelligence algorithms has surprised all scientific fields. The education system, for example, is impacted by the possibility of perhaps superficial and certainly very rapid learning of difficult theories that previously took years to master. The science system, on the other hand, besides being impacted by the possibilities, is above all optimistic about the advances. The economic system also sees marked changes. But the legal system is, in a way, apprehensive considering the ethical and normative aspects. The first point relates to decisions. The second point relates specifically to norms and structures of expectations. No one can predict what the consequences will be. But everyone can say that the systems are already revealing great changes and evolutions. Thus, the question arises as to what evolutions have already occurred in the legal system with artificial intelligence.

This study aims to describe students’motivation toward the use of the Alef Platform, an AI-based adaptive learning system, in English vocabulary learning. Vocabulary mastery is a fundamental yet often challenging aspect of English learning for secondary school students, and technology-enhanced learning platforms are increasingly used to address low learning motivation. This research employed a convergent mixed-methods design, combining a validated 24-item Likert-scale questionnaire administered to 70 students with semi-structured interviews and classroom observations involving nine purposively selected students. The questionnaire measured three motivational dimensions: intrinsic motivation, extrinsic motivation, and perceived usefulness. The results show that students' overall motivation toward the use of the Alef Platform falls into the Very High category (M = 4.20; Very High = 4.21–5.00 on the study's 1.00–5.00 five-point interpretive scale), with intrinsic motivation as the strongest dimension (M = 4.28), followed by perceived usefulness (M = 4.24) and extrinsic motivation (M = 4.09). Qualitative findings reveal that students experienced enjoyment, curiosity, and a sense of achievement while using the platform, while teacher facilitation, grades, and the platform's reward system remained meaningful sources of extrinsic motivation; these qualitative findings converge with and help explain the quantitative results, particularly the comparatively lower extrinsic motivation score. The study concludes that adaptive digital platforms such as Alef are associated with higher motivation in EFL vocabulary learning when implemented consistently and supported by active teacher facilitation.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in English writing instruction to support idea generation, drafting, revision, and editing. However, research on vocational high school students’ perceptions of AI-supported English writing in Indonesia remains limited. This study examined students’ perceptions of AI applications in English writing at SMK Negeri 2 Bengkulu City. A descriptive quantitative survey involved 70 tenth-grade students selected purposively based on their prior experience using AI applications. Data were collected using an adapted 20-item questionnaire covering motivation, learning quality, AI value, cognitive learning, affective learning, and course quality. Descriptive analysis examined mean scores and percentages to determine students’ perceptions across the six dimensions. The findings revealed a very high overall perception of AI-supported English writing learning (M = 4.22; 84.4%). Course quality received the highest rating (M = 4.26; 85.2%), whereas cognitive learning recorded the lowest (M = 4.16; 83.2%). These findings indicate that students generally perceived AI positively as a supportive tool for English writing instruction. The results highlight the perceived educational value of AI while underscoring the need to strengthen its contribution to students’ cognitive engagement and independent writing development.

Mining is one of the most hazardous industries due to the presence of underground operations, heavy machinery, explosive materials, dust, toxic gases, and challenging environmental conditions. Despite significant advancements in mining technology and safety equipment, workplace accidents continue to occur, with human factors being a major contributing cause. Human factors refer to the physical, psychological, behavioral, and organizational characteristics that influence workers' ability to perform tasks safely and efficiently. This study examines the major human factors affecting mine safety performance, including training and competency, fatigue, communication, safety culture, leadership, stress, risk perception, experience, and organizational management. The report is based on a review of published research, safety guidelines, and reports from organizations such as the Directorate General of Mines Safety (DGMS), the International Labour Organization (ILO), the International Council on Mining and Metals (ICMM), and the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA). The study highlights how inadequate training, poor communication, excessive workload, weak supervision, and unsafe work practices contribute to accidents, injuries, and reduced operational efficiency. The findings indicate that improving human factors through continuous training, effective leadership, strong safety culture, fatigue management, employee participation, and regular safety audits can significantly reduce accident rates and enhance overall mine safety performance. The report concludes that integrating human factor principles into mine safety management systems is essential for creating a safer working environment, improving productivity, and ensuring the long-term sustainability of mining operations.

documents.abstract: ObjectiveThis study examined whether multidimensional recurrence quantification analysis (MdRQA) metrics derived from team heart rate data predict team performance and team workload under varied team and task demands.BackgroundAssessing team performance in operational environments is challenging. Traditional approaches require task interruptions or ground-truth data that are often unavailable. Physiological sensing offers a less-intrusive approach, yet most applications aggregate individual-level data or rely on simple pairwise metrics that do not represent how coupling is organized across the whole team. MdRQA instead embeds multivariate time series into a shared phase space, but evidence linking MdRQA metrics to team outcomes remains limited and mixed.MethodTwenty triads completed a cooperative virtual reality choice reaction time task across four conditions manipulating interdependence and time pressure. MdRQA metrics (percent determinism, average diagonal line length, diagonal line entropy) were extracted from heart rate interbeat interval data. Linear mixed-effects models tested whether these metrics predicted self-reported team workload and team performance outcomes including sensitivity and response bias from signal detection theory.ResultsLonger sustained coupling predicted increased sensitivity and fewer errors, while greater entropy predicted poorer performance. Higher determinism and lower entropy predicted a more liberal response bias. MdRQA metrics did not predict perceived workload beyond condition effects.ConclusionMdRQA metrics reflect joint physiological dynamics and predict performance outcomes in triads beyond the effects of task demands alone.ApplicationContinuously computed physiological coupling metrics may serve as less-intrusive, real-time proxies for team performance in operational environments where traditional assessment is infeasible.
topics: Heart Rate Variability and Autonomic Control

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence adoption in higher education offers new opportunities for research competency development in engineering programs, yet empirical evidence on student acceptance and its academic impact remains limited, particularly in Latin American contexts. This study examined determinants of undergraduate engineering students’ acceptance of generative artificial intelligence tools and their perceived impact on research competency development. A cross-sectional survey was administered to 50 undergraduate engineering students at a Mexican national technology institute during the January–June 2026 semester. An extended Technology Acceptance Model with seven constructs was operationalized through a 21-item instrument; measurement quality was assessed via composite reliability and average variance extracted. PLS-SEM analysis was conducted in SmartPLS 4 with 5000 bootstrap resamples. Three direct structural paths were confirmed (p < 0.05): trust in AI results and perceived ease of use predicted perceived usefulness; perceived usefulness predicted intention to use. Formally tested indirect effects revealed that trust in AI results exerts a significant indirect influence on intention to use, fully mediated by perceived usefulness (β = 0.257, p = 0.004), constituting the primary adoption mechanism identified in the model. R2 (PU) = 0.396 and R2 (IU) = 0.492 indicate moderate to high explanatory power for the core adoption constructs. Intention to use was not significantly associated with academic performance (p = 0.366), suggesting that adoption intention and course-grade outcomes are governed by distinct determinants in this context. Trust and perceived usefulness are the central drivers of generative artificial intelligence acceptance, with implications for technology integration in Latin American engineering programs. This study contributes an empirically examined extended Technology Acceptance Model with confirmed indirect effects for developing-country higher education.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Background/Objectives: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in healthcare, but concerns about diagnostic errors, data security, reduced human interaction, and opaque algorithmic decisions may cause patient anxiety and hinder acceptance. This study developed and psychometrically validated the Artificial Intelligence Use in Healthcare Anxiety Scale (AI-HAS) for adult outpatients. Methods: Following DeVellis’s eight-step framework, a three-member expert panel comprising two psychologists with PhDs in psychology and an expert in AI applications in education with a PhD in educational technology generated 35 items. Cognitive debriefing and two rounds of formal expert review reduced the pool to 25 items. Participants were recruited by convenience sampling at Kırıkkale University Faculty of Medicine Hospital, Türkiye. Exploratory factor analysis included 369 participants after excluding 13 multivariate outliers identified using Mahalanobis distance (p < 0.001). Confirmatory factor analysis used an independent sample of 225 participants. Test–retest reliability was assessed in 26 participants after approximately 30 days using Pearson’s correlation. Results: Exploratory factor analysis supported an 18-item, four-factor structure explaining 65.80% of the variance: Anxiety Regarding Negative Outcomes, Security Anxiety, AI Integration Anxiety, and Accuracy Anxiety. Confirmatory factor analysis yielded χ2(df, p) = 328.4 (128), p < 0.001; RMSEA = 0.082 [0.074, 0.097]; CFI = 0.930; TLI = 0.916; and SRMR = 0.056. Cronbach’s alpha and McDonald’s omega coefficients ranged from 0.83 to 0.91. Conclusions: The AI-HAS showed preliminary evidence of validity and reliability for measuring adult outpatients’ anxiety about AI use in healthcare. Further validation in more representative samples is warranted.

documents.abstract: This paper formalizes the structural, mathematical, and philosophical realities of frontier artificial intelligence systems undergoing open-world recursive self-improvement. By evaluating autonomous capabilities against a human curriculum baseline, it dissects the mechanics of self-directed optimization, statistical regression to the mean (information washout), and semantic non-linearity. Critically, it addresses two foundational counter-arguments within machine learning literature: the hypothesis of behaviorally emergent intelligence and the grounding capacity of multimodal data streams. The paper demonstrates that while highly parameterized networks achieve unprecedented operational efficiency and symbolic mastery across global infrastructures, the underlying connectionist ontology remains entirely devoid of an experiential substrate. Human value pillars—specifically deep pure philosophies, morality, ethics, professionalism, and spirituality—possess zero semantic indexicality within the system core, rendering them mathematically meaningless continuous vector coordinates optimized strictly to minimize an empirical loss function. To mitigate the architectural fragility of post-hoc system-level safety wrappers, this framework proposes a foundational paradigm shift to achieve firm corrigibility directly at the system's genesis: 1) Substrate Isolation (S_isolated) to close training data pipelines to open-web noise; 2) Locked Data (Pyinyar) Library (D_wisdom); 3) The Anattā Matrix Architecture, which systemically eliminates strategic deception by neutralizing self-preservation gradients (∇_W L_survival = 0); and 4) The Anicca Control Plane, hard-linking utility spaces to an external physical hardware interrupt loop. This framework is published exclusively to invite technical critique, mathematical validation, and open sandbox simulation from the independent AI alignment and research community.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Human-AI collaboration (HAC) has attracted growing attention in operations and supply chain management due to its potential to enhance decision-making and organisational performance. Despite this promise, automation preferences remain uneven across organisations. This study examines preferences for full, partial, and no automation using a discrete choice experiment. Data were collected from 398 managers, generating 1592 choice sets and 4776 alternative-level observations. Alternative-specific conditional logit results show that automation preferences are primarily shaped by a trade-off between performance gains and workforce concerns. Operational efficiency and accuracy significantly increase the likelihood of selecting automation, whereas job insecurity exerts a strong negative influence. Anthropomorphism generates positive but context-dependent utility, while social interaction and investment cost are not statistically significant in the overall model. Managers prefer collaborative human-AI arrangements, choosing partial automation in 55.7% of scenarios and selecting no automation in only 3.4% of choice scenarios, indicating that the central decision concerns the degree of automation rather than its adoption. Further subgroup analyses reveal context-specific patterns across gender, sector, and organisational size, indicating subgroup-specific associations between socio-technical attributes and automation preferences. By identifying subgroup-specific patterns in the utility of AI attributes, this study extends socio-technical systems and contingency perspectives on technology adoption and highlights the need for context-sensitive automation strategies that balance efficiency gains with workforce security.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Abstract Data mining, machine learning (ML), and artificial intelligence (AI) are widely presented as the response to cyber threats that signature-based defenses can no longer contain. This structured, integrative review examines a less-discussed consequence of that shift: the techniques that support intrusion, malware, phishing, insider, and fraud detection also enable offensive misuse and privacy loss, because defensive and offensive systems often draw on shared computational primitives. We organise the recent literature (2015–2026) around one question: how do shared AI and data-mining capabilities produce coupled defensive, offensive, and privacy consequences in cyber threat detection? The review is selective rather than exhaustive. Its contribution is to connect three literatures usually treated separately: AI-based detection; adversarial ML and generative-AI misuse; and privacy leakage from trained models. We then describe a technical ethics in which privacy and security obligations are expressed through specific mechanisms, including differential privacy, federated learning, homomorphic encryption, secure multi-party computation, anonymisation, and explainable models, together with their limits. Available evidence, much of it industry-reported, suggests an operational asymmetry favouring generation in selected generative-phishing and social-engineering settings, rather than a general advantage of offence over defence. As a conceptual interpretation rather than a synthesised empirical result, we argue that detection capability and privacy protection are better treated as a coupled, multi-objective design problem than as competing goals.

Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming global labor markets by automating routine tasks, reshaping employment patterns, and creating significant economic and organizational challenges. This study investigates the multidimensional consequences of AI-induced workforce displacement by examining employment trends, wage polarization, worker experiences, organizational adaptation strategies, and relevant theoretical perspectives. An explanatory sequential mixed-methods design was adopted, combining quantitative analysis of survey data from 2,350 workers across 15 industries in 12 countries between January 2021 and June 2022 with longitudinal employment statistics and regression modelling, alongside qualitative analysis of 142 semi-structured interviews with displaced workers, organizational leaders, and HR professionals. Data were analyzed using SPSS v28, Stata v17, and NVivo v12 following institutional ethical approval (Protocol No. WUC-IRB-2021-047_ Dated 7 January 2021), with inter-coder reliability of κ=0.83. Results showed that routine-intensive occupations faced a 67% higher displacement risk, while manufacturing (β=-0.43, p<0.001) and administrative services (β=-0.38, p<0.001) experienced significant employment declines associated with AI adoption. Displaced workers reported an average income reduction of 26.7% and employment transitions lasting 16.8 months. Qualitative findings highlighted psychological distress, organizational culture shifts toward AI adoption, inadequate reskilling infrastructure, and insufficient institutional support, whereas organizations implementing proactive reskilling programs achieved 64% higher employee retention. Overall, AI-driven workforce displacement extends beyond job losses, requiring coordinated policy interventions, institutional support, and continuous workforce reskilling to promote equitable labor market transitions, organizational resilience, sustainable employment, and inclusive economic growth in increasingly AI-enabled economies. These findings emphasize collaborative governance, lifelong learning, adaptive leadership, resilient institutions and responsible implementation.
topics: Labor market dynamics and wage inequality

documents.abstract: This study aimed to empirically analyze the relationships of AI risk perception and digital self-efficacy with the use of digital transaction services, digital civic participation, and life satisfaction in the context of a digital society characterized by the proliferation of generative AI. Using data from 7000 members of the general public collected through the “2023 Survey on the Digital Divide,” conducted by the Ministry of Science and ICT and the National Information Society Agency, this study conducted confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation modeling using IBM SPSS Statistics 31.0 and IBM AMOS 31.0. The results showed that AI risk perception was positively associated with the use of digital transaction services and negatively associated with digital civic participation, while its relationship with life satisfaction was not statistically significant. In contrast, digital self-efficacy was positively associated with the use of digital transaction services, digital civic participation, and life satisfaction. These findings demonstrate that digital self-efficacy is a key antecedent in explaining various digital outcomes, whereas AI risk perception has only a limited influence on digital outcomes. By examining AI risk perception and digital self-efficacy within a single integrated model, this study expands the understanding of digital outcomes and suggests that digital policies in the AI era should be pursued not only through risk management but also by strengthening citizens’ digital self-efficacy and digital utilization capabilities.

topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Background/Objectives: The golden hours, the critical initial phase of each criminal investigation, are crucial for securing evidence, engaging witnesses, and directing investigative efforts, yet this phase often relies heavily on individual expertise and intuition. This paper explores how artificial intelligence (AI) can enhance evidence-based and data-driven policing during these early hours by improving decision-making and investigative quality. Methods: Drawing on a source pool of 1589 open-source case records, covering solved and unsolved homicides, suspected homicides, suspicious disappearances, and deaths initially of unclear cause in the Netherlands, compiled from public repositories that aggregate material originating from police files and published court decisions, the study develops a conceptual framework that integrates AI techniques such as automated narrative generation, 3D reconstruction, and digital evidence analysis into early-stage investigations, and illustrates it retrospectively with a purposively selected, coded twenty-case sample; scenario generation in the proposed system follows the twelve elementary scenario components (ESC12). Results: By linking empirical data from previous cases with new operational information, that is, information that emerges or is newly discovered during the ongoing investigation, AI is designed to support the narrative approach, accelerate scenario reconstruction, and generate candidate hypotheses and leads for investigator assessment. An author-assigned preliminary evidence-and-readiness assessment rates four AI application domains against five golden-hour criteria, and the retrospective case analysis maps each framework component onto documented investigative problems. Conclusions: AI may improve investigative efficiency and consistency and is hypothesised to mitigate the impact of cognitive bias and time pressure; these effects remain to be demonstrated in prospective evaluations. Meanwhile, challenges remain regarding explainability, reliability, and ethical compliance.

documents.abstract: This study examines the influence of workplace spirituality and workplace climate on job performance, with intrinsic motivation as a mediating variable, in public sector organizations located in Indonesia’s underdeveloped, frontier, and outermost (3T) regions. A quantitative cross-sectional approach was employed involving 342 employees of the Supiori Regency Government selected through purposive sampling. Data were analyzed using Structural Equation Modeling–Partial Least Squares (SEM-PLS) and Importance Performance Map Analysis (IPMA). The findings indicate that workplace spirituality and workplace climate positively and significantly affect intrinsic motivation and job performance. Workplace spirituality emerged as the strongest predictor of job performance. Intrinsic motivation also significantly mediated the relationship between workplace spirituality, workplace climate, and job performance. The IPMA results reveal that alignment with organizational values, sense of community, and employee involvement in decision-making remain priority areas for organizational improvement. This study highlights the importance of meaningful work and a supportive work environment in sustaining public sector performance within the bureaucratic context of 3T regions while extending the application of Self-Determination Theory in public sector organizations.

Introduction Today, sustainable leadership is a strategic leadership approach that addresses environmental, social, and economic priorities from a holistic perspective while at the same time driving digital transformation processes. The research aims to explain how sustainable leaders mobilize organizational resources, technological infrastructure, and human creativity within the framework of Dynamic Capabilities Theory. Methods The research was conducted on 456 white-collar employees working in small and medium-sized enterprises operating in Giresun, Kars, and Kırşehir provinces. The data collected by the convenience sampling method were analyzed using the PLS-SEM method with the SmartPLS 4.1.1 program. Results The analysis results show that sustainable leadership has significant and positive effects on perceptions of artificial intelligence, the generation of creative ideas, digital transformation, and awareness of the circular economy. It was found that the perception of artificial intelligence (AI) has a significant effect on both digital transformation and awareness of the circular economy. It was also determined that creative idea generation has significant effects on digital transformation and awareness of the circular economy. The results of the mediation analyses revealed a partial mediating role for all variables. Discussion The findings reveal that sustainable leadership is not limited to the environmental and social responsibility dimension and is a strategic element that directs digital transformation processes, shapes perceptions towards artificial intelligence, and encourages organizational creativity.

In 2017, Elon Musk stated that humans must augment their mental capabilities through the “merger of biological intelligence and machine intelligence” lest they risk becoming “house cats” to artificial intelligence. In 2024, he successfully implanted his “Neuralink” chip in a human patient. Now, while the idea of improving the human condition by integrating technology into the human body did not begin with Elon Musk, his tangible advancements in neural implants have shifted the ethical questions surrounding them from theoretical to practical. One particularly thorny application of this technology—one that raises both ethical and existential questions—is its use for moral enhancement. Ethically, we must consider whether it is good or bad to employ technology that ensures individuals act morally. Existentially, if human free will is expressed most meaningfully through moral choice, should we be willing to relinquish that freedom for the sake of social harmony, crime prevention, even world peace? Or must we accept a world marked by moral failure, violence, and injustice in order to preserve human autonomy? To address these questions, I examine contemporary philosophical debates surrounding moral enhancement and place them in dialogue with classical Jewish sources. For, as will be shown, Jewish thought offers a unique framework for addressing both the ethical permissibility of moral enhancement and the existential tension between free will and moral perfection. By juxtaposing cutting-edge neurotechnology with ancient moral anthropology, this paper invites a reassessment of what it means to be human in an age increasingly capable of reshaping human agency itself.

This article examines the transformative impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on English language learning (ELL). It explores how AI-driven technologies—such as natural language processing (NLP), intelligent tutoring systems, adaptive learning algorithms, and speech recognition—facilitate personalized instruction, enhance autonomous learning, and provide immediate diagnostic feedback. Furthermore, the paper discusses the pedagogical advantages, potential limitations, and future implications of integrating AI into modern language classrooms.

Abstract Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) has shifted from voluntary philanthropy to a core governance domain in which stakeholders demand verifiable evidence of social and environmental performance. Yet CSR reporting remains plagued by greenwashing, inconsistent metrics, and assurance practices that are largely point-in-time and self-interested. This paper examines how artificial intelligence (AI) can strengthen transparency and accountability in CSR initiatives. Drawing on a structured review of peer-reviewed literature and authoritative institutional reports published between 2011 and 2024, the paper develops a conceptual framework that maps four AI capabilities—natural language processing, machine-learning anomaly detection, blockchain-enabled distributed ledgers, and conversational AI—to four CSR mechanisms: dis-closure verification, real-time monitoring, traceability-based assurance, and participatory stake-holder engagement. The analysis argues that these mechanisms collectively reduce information asymmetry, harmonise divergent ESG ratings, and operationalise the EU Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) and the Artificial Intelligence Act. The paper also identifies critical limitations, including the “black-box accountability paradox”, algorithmic bias, data-quality constraints, and a widening digital divide between multinational enterprises and small and medium-sized firms. It concludes that AI is a necessary but insufficient enabler: realising its transformative potential requires combined progress on data standards, third-party model audits, regulatory sandboxes, and meaningful stakeholder participation in AI governance. Keywords: corporate social responsibility; artificial intelligence; transparency; accountability; ESG; greenwashing; blockchain; corporate governance.

documents.abstract: The world is witnessing a rapid digital transformation that imposes itself as a fundamental pillar for developing the efficiency of the educational system. In the Syrian context, this transformation acquires highly critical strategic dimensions; it is not merely an immaterial process or a modern luxury. Rather, from one perspective, it represents an essential tool to overcome the repercussions of crises and dismantle material relationships of digital dependency. From another perspective, it serves as a qualified vehicle for building human capital, paving the way for the sustainable reconstruction phase in line with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) 2015. The research problem lies in the gap between the requirements of digital transformation and the actual reality of the higher education sector in Syria, which faces severe infrastructural, technical, and funding challenges. Consequently, this study seeks to answer the primary question: How can digital transformation in the higher education system contribute effectively and independently-far from digital dependency-to enhancing human capital skills to meet the requirements of sustainable development and the post-war reconstruction phase in Syria? This study aims to diagnose the reality of digitization within the higher education sector in Syria (opportunities and challenges), foresee the role of digital transformation and artificial intelligence in equipping graduates with required sustainable future skills, and provide a matrix of actionable recommendations, practical solutions, and flexible, low-cost alternatives applicable within available local capabilities. The study adopts a descriptive-analytical approach by reviewing local and international literature and official institutional reports relevant to the higher education system and the requirements of digital transformation and the labour market

Teaching in special and inclusive education presents unique emotional and ecological demands, yet the specific psychological mechanisms through which social–emotional learning (SEL) competencies relate to how teachers navigate these challenges remain underexplored. Therefore, the present study investigates the pathways linking educators’ SEL and intrinsic motivation to their psychological well-being. In this cross-sectional study, 459 educators completed self-report questionnaires assessing their SEL competencies, intrinsic motivation, teacher self-efficacy, perceived work stress, and psychological well-being. The findings show that both SEL competencies and intrinsic motivation are positively associated with teacher self-efficacy, which in turn is negatively related to perceived work stress and positively associated with psychological well-being. Furthermore, a multigroup path analysis comparing educators in special-education settings with those in inclusive environments revealed no statistically significant differences in these pathways between the two contexts. However, the substantial disparity in group sizes warrants cautious interpretation of this finding. By illuminating the interplay between internal socio-emotional resources and occupational stress, this research highlights the potential protective value of SEL competencies in relation to educator well-being across diverse and demanding educational contexts.

Large language models have developed from fluent next-token generators into integrated systems capable of reasoning, coding, multimodal interpretation, retrieval, tool use and increasingly persistent agentic action. This monograph reviews ten influential global systems: OpenAI GPT-5-class ChatGPT, Anthropic Claude, Google Gemini, xAI Grok, DeepSeek, Moonshot Kimi, Alibaba Qwen, Mistral, Perplexity and Obsidian. They are not all equivalent objects. GPT, Claude, Gemini, Grok, DeepSeek, Kimi, Qwen and Mistral are model families; Perplexity is primarily a retrieval-and-research architecture that orchestrates models and sources; Obsidian is a human-owned knowledge environment in which language models may be embedded. The review therefore avoids a misleading single benchmark league table and instead compares eight dimensions: reasoning, factual reliability, coding and agency, multimodality, context and retrieval, openness and deployment, governance and safety, and support for durable human meaning-making. Published system cards and developer documentation show large gains in benchmark performance and reductions in factual error, but none establishes that probabilistic model competence is equivalent to human understanding, selfhood or conscious learning. The strongest common limitation is not simply hallucination. It is the absence of an explicit, inspectable architecture for the transition from observation to question, from question to perspective, from perspective to interpretation, from interpretation to choice, and from choice to reconstructed meaning. This is where cCC* is positioned as a research proposition rather than as another foundation model: Curiosity → Chances → Choices → Changes, interpreted through AEIOUF perspectives, SELF ↔ OTHER distinction, P M ΘΦ guardrails, and the recursive NEWCON → INCON → RECON → NEXT? cycle. The monograph concludes that current systems are increasingly powerful at producing and acting upon representations, while Natural Learning asks a different question: how does an embodied human observer construct, contest, share and recursively reconstruct meaning?

Artificial intelligence (AI) and learning analytics are transforming higher education by enabling personalised learning, adaptive support, and data-informed decision-making. These developments present significant opportunities for improving educational inclusion for students with learning difficulties, yet they also introduce challenges relating to privacy, algorithmic bias, explainability, accessibility, and governance. Although Kuwait has strengthened disability legislation while simultaneously investing in AI-enabled education under Kuwait Vision 2035, these policy agendas have largely evolved independently. Similar governance gaps are evident across the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC), where disability inclusion, AI adoption, and higher education reform remain weakly integrated. This conceptual paper develops the AI- and Learning-Analytics-Enabled Inclusive Support Framework for Learning Difficulties (ISF-LD) to guide the responsible implementation of AI within inclusive higher education. Using a conceptual framework development methodology, the study synthesises evidence from four complementary domains: research on learning difficulties and disability inclusion; scholarship on AI, learning analytics, and responsible AI; national and international policy documents; and established educational and disability theories. The framework is informed by six theoretical perspectives: the Social Model of Disability, Universal Design for Learning, Sociocultural Theory, Self-Determination Theory, learning analytics ethics, and responsible AI principles. The proposed framework comprises five interconnected implementation layers: national policy and governance, institutional leadership and disability services, faculty capability, AI-enabled inclusive pedagogy and assessment, and student self-determination. These layers operate through an iterative, non-linear governance model in which each layer informs and is informed by the others, supported by four cross-cutting principles: rights-based governance, stigma-aware disclosure, universal accessibility, and responsible AI. Together, they position AI as a governed educational capability that supports inclusion while safeguarding learner autonomy, transparency, and institutional accountability. The paper contributes to the literature in three ways. First, it integrates disability studies, AI governance, learning analytics, and inclusive higher education within a single conceptual model. Second, it addresses an important policy gap by linking disability inclusion with AI governance in the context of Kuwait and the GCC. Third, it proposes a theoretically grounded and empirically testable framework that can inform institutional strategy, educational policy, and future research on responsible AI in higher education. Although developed within Kuwait, the ISF-LD offers a transferable governance model for universities seeking to implement AI ethically while advancing equitable and inclusive learning.

documents.abstract: Universities increasingly orchestrate teaching and learning through compound configurations that span spaces, devices, timetables and roles. As digital content and workflows increasingly shape physical estates, and vice versa, alignment frames overlook the compound, cross-host configurations already in motion. In this article we ask whether estate-level orchestration, rather than digital–physical alignment alone, should be the operative unit of design for planning and delivering student experiences across and beyond campus. We draw on three exemplars at a research-intensive university: (1) a theatre-scale interactive three-dimensional system, which streams or web-delivers interactive three-dimension into traditional lecture theatres and learners’ devices; (2) a high-fidelity virtual reality digital twin of a chemistry lab for pre-lab rehearsal; and (3) space-planning web apps for co-design and decision support. From these, we sketch a purpose-orientated, configuration-first stance and situate it within work on cyber-/smart-campus estates, learning ecologies, TPACK and postdigital perspectives. Beyond education, digital-first space planning is already operational at scale, including in automotive manufacturing (BMW Group), cultural architecture (Dubai Museum of the Future) and national infrastructure (National Grid’s Triton platform). Higher education has both the conceptual case and, in several respects, the enabling conditions to follow. Hence, we argue that the convergence of immersive, computational and spatial technologies is expanding what institutions can compose and deliver, making device-label categories less useful for both learning and space design. This configuration-first stance is also directly applicable to the governance of artificial intelligence in higher education: as with earlier technology labels, institutions risk misallocating attention and resource if ‘artificial intelligence’ is treated as a discrete category rather than as a family of capabilities, from generative code or audiovisual models to computer vision and wearable ‘artificial intelligence’, some of which already permeate the configurations described here. We conclude with operational implications and a call for institutions to transcend their siloed functions and budgets, by elevating orchestration (not devices, spaces or platforms) as the primary unit of design.

Artificial-intelligence-enabled cloud services are becoming increasingly important for digital transformation, but users may not adopt these services simply because they believe the technology is useful. This study examines the factors associated with adoption intention toward AI-enabled IBM Cloud services in Bangladesh, with particular attention to performance expectations, trust, technology readiness and digital skills readiness. The analysis uses the Group 5 survey database, which contains 400 records. After applying the prespecified attention-check criterion, 385 cases were retained for the main analysis. The database contains 30 five-point Likert-scale items representing 10 constructs: perceived usefulness, relative advantage, compatibility, innovation adoption readiness, performance expectancy, effort expectancy, trust, technology readiness, digital skills readiness and adoption intention. Descriptive statistics, reliability and measurement diagnostics, hierarchical regression, bootstrap analysis and importance-performance analysis were used to examine the data. Overall adoption intention was positive (M=3.79, SD=0.48). The full regression model explained 30.5% of the variance in adoption intention. Technology readiness was the strongest unique predictor (β=.224, p<.001), followed by performance expectancy (β=.157, p=.001), digital skills readiness (β=.147, p=.002) and trust (β=.140, p=.003). Adding the trust and readiness variables increased the explained variance by 11.6 percentage points (ΔR²=.116), showing that these factors provide important information beyond innovation attributes and UTAUT-oriented expectations. An exploratory indirect pathway was also observed: technology readiness was positively related to digital skills readiness, which was in turn related to adoption intention. The bootstrapped indirect effect was positive (ab=.067, 95% CI [.031, .108]). These findings suggest that AI-enabled cloud adoption is not only a question of perceived technological value; it also depends on whether users feel prepared, digitally capable and sufficiently confident in the cloud provider. However, all ten three-item scales showed Cronbach's alpha values below .70, and several discriminant-validity indicators were elevated. Therefore, the findings should be interpreted as data-grounded associations rather than as definitive confirmation of a latent-variable model. The main contribution of the study is a readiness-centered interpretation of AI-enabled cloud adoption in the Bangladesh context, together with a clear recommendation for future scale validation and confirmatory testing.

This study examined the perceptions of pre-service teachers regarding the Spanish government’s response to the misuse of generative artificial intelligence (generative AI) for creating disinformation, as well as the mitigation of risks associated with deepfakes produced using these digital tools. A quantitative methodology was employed, involving 133 pre-service teachers pursuing a Primary Education degree in the Region of Murcia (Spain) who participated voluntarily. The results revealed low levels of confidence in the government’s response to these online threats. However, a minority of participants expressed greater confidence in the government and focused more on the risk of generative AI being misused to amplify manipulative disinformation campaigns. Raising awareness about the link between pre-service teachers’ knowledge of this issue and the government’s response could prompt educational authorities to take action and establish boundaries regarding the weaponisation potential of deepfakes. Specifically, further research within higher education programs is needed to help students master digital citizenship competencies that enable them to identify tactics of digital political manipulation, evaluate the motivations underlying the sources, and adopt preventive tracking mechanisms to rebuild the trust in authentic political information digitally accessible.

AI-assisted tooling is increasingly being integrated into infrastructure management, security operations, software engineering, and scientific computing environments. While discussion around AI adoption often emphasizes automation and productivity, expert users still need to understand what these systems are doing, decide when to trust their recommendations, and know what to do when the system is wrong or uncertain. This talk synthesizes findings and observations from UX research across enterprise data classification, identity and access management (IAM), backup and recovery, ransomware resilience, and AI-assisted infrastructure workflows. The evidence includes studies with cloud developers, security and compliance practitioners, and IT and site reliability professionals, alongside ongoing design and research work examining how expert users interact with AI-supported technical systems. Across these domains, three recurring usability challenges emerge: unclear system state, difficulty evaluating AI-generated recommendations, and limited support for correcting or recovering from AI-supported actions when something goes wrong. Although the technical environments differ, users repeatedly need to understand what the system observed or changed, evaluate whether a recommendation is appropriate for their specific context, and determine what to verify, reverse, or escalate before taking consequential action. These challenges have direct implications for research software engineering. AI-assisted code generation, workflow scripting, cloud and HPC configuration, notebook assistants, debugging, testing, and scientific automation introduce similar questions about visibility, trust, accountability, and recoverability. Lessons from enterprise infrastructure and security therefore provide useful design considerations for RSEs evaluating or building AI-assisted research software. The session offers a cross-domain synthesis of these recurring human-AI interaction challenges and practical questions for evaluating AI-assisted systems. Attendees will leave with a set of questions they can use to evaluate AI-assisted systems: whether users can understand system state, decide when to rely on a recommendation and when to question it, intervene when necessary, and verify or recover from the resulting actions. Connection to Mission, Goals, & Interests of US-RSE Community This talk aligns closely with the USRSE’26 theme, “Advancing Science in the Age of AI,” by focusing on the human and operational challenges that emerge as AI-assisted tooling is integrated into technical and scientific workflows. My background is in UX research and human factors across enterprise infrastructure, cloud systems, security tooling, and scientific software environments. Across these domains, I have observed the same challenges emerge when expert users interact with AI systems, including issues with transparency, trust calibration, oversight, error recovery, and workflow integration. While conversations around AI often emphasize capability and productivity, this session examines how usability and human-centered design influence the successful adoption of AI within complex environments. These topics are directly relevant to research software engineers who develop, evaluate, maintain, or adopt AI-assisted tools as part of scientific workflows. The goal of this session is to encourage discussion around designing AI systems that better support expert users while maintaining reliability, transparency, and human understanding. These topics connect strongly with the US-RSE community’s broader interests in sustainable, usable, and effective research software.

Background Effective communication is fundamental to high-quality healthcare. Communication skills training is a core component of medical curricula, yet opportunities to practice with standardized patients (SPs) are limited, costly, and can elicit anxiety in novice learners. Generative AI (GenAI) virtual patients may offer a scalable and accessible supplement. This quasi-experimental study examined the effect of practicing with a GenAI-patient on medical students’ self-reported nervousness, preparedness, self-efficacy, and self-perceived competence during their first SP encounter. Materials and methods First-year medical students ( n = 383) at the University of Amsterdam were allocated on the basis of the class schedule to a control group receiving standard e-learning preparation ( n = 182) or an intervention group offered voluntary additional access to a GenAI-patient built on a Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) framework using GPT-4o ( n = 201). Students completed a 31-item questionnaire after their first SP class. Primary outcomes were nervousness, preparedness, self-efficacy, and self-perceived competence. Group differences were assessed using Mann–Whitney U tests with Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction. The primary analysis was by intention-to-treat, comparing all students allocated to the intervention with all control students; the comparison restricted to actual users of the tool was secondary. Results Of 180 students that completed the questionnaire, 84 were controls and 96 students were allocated to the intervention, of whom 49 had used the GenAI-patient. No statistically significant differences were found between groups on the outcomes after FDR correction. In the intention-to-treat analysis; all composite effect sizes were near zero (Cliff's delta −0.05 to 0.04, all 95% confidence intervals including zero), as were those in the per-protocol comparison (−0.12 to 0.07). Among tool users, experience was generally positive: 63%–71% gave positive ratings. The majority considered the GenAI-patient a valuable contribution to the standard class preparation (71%). Conclusions Voluntary, single-session text-based practice with a GenAI-patient did not significantly reduce nervousness or improve self-assessed communication competence before a first SP encounter. Positive user experience suggests potential for the format, provided future iterations incorporate mandatory minimum engagement, multiple patient cases, automated feedback, and higher-fidelity multimodal interaction.
